node.label: Amy Kaplan
node.date_label: The Social Construction of American Realism (1988) · Cultures of United States Imperialism, coedited (1993) · Manifest Domesticity (1998) · The Anarchy of Empire (2002) · Our American Israel (2018)
node.description: Amy Kaplan argued in The Anarchy of Empire in the Making of U.S. Culture (2002) that imperial expansion abroad, from the U.S.–Mexican War to the First World War, profoundly shaped American culture at home. Her essay Manifest Domesticity (1998) treated the home and women’s domestic role as active parts of national expansion. With Donald E. Pease she coedited Cultures of United States Imperialism (1993), calling for the study of American culture to confront empire and for postcolonial studies to include the United States. Kristin Hoganson later credited these writings with helping her develop cultural histories of masculinity, consumption and imperial power. Reception also exposed disagreements about method and scope. In 2004 Dolores Janiewski praised Kaplan’s interdisciplinary readings but criticized the limited historical contextualization of Twain’s writings on race and empire; Anders Stephanson disputed the book’s anarchy frame while admiring its individual readings. Ann Laura Stoler treated Kaplan’s account of scholarly absences as illuminating for an earlier historiography but argued that subsequent work had begun to bridge those gaps. Kaplan’s later essays on Guantánamo and Our American Israel (2018) extended her inquiry into the cultural and legal relations through which American power was made intelligible.

proposed_edges.relationship: McAlister’s 2021 remembrance identifies Said as an influence on Kaplan’s cultural study of imperialism, while describing The Anarchy of Empire (2002) as partly departing from Orientalism’s account of imperial coherence.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Melani McAlister, Passport (January 2021), printed pp. 65–66: identifies Said as an influence and then qualifies Kaplan’s later relation to his model of imperial coherence. Both passages read in the society’s PDF. This is McAlister’s interpretation, not a direct reading of Kaplan’s or Said’s books; retain the Said → Kaplan influence edge with the departure explicit in its sentence.

proposed_edges.relationship: Manifest Domesticity (1998) made domesticity part of the explanation of U.S. imperial expansion, reading the home through its relation to the foreign as well as to men’s public sphere.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Hoganson, H-Diplo, printed p. 10, paragraphs beginning Her 1998 essay and Although my own research, with note 19; corroborated by McAlister, Passport, p. 66, opening two paragraphs. These named scholarly readers explain the argument and its use in gender history. The 1998 original, pp. 581–606, remains unread; no claim to have checked its complete sequence of examples.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Left Alone with America (1993), Kaplan criticized the omission of U.S. empire from postcolonial studies and urged reading national culture through internal and external colonization together.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Hoganson, H-Diplo, printed p. 9, paragraph beginning The publication of Cultures, specifically its account of Kaplan’s introduction. This is an explicitly attributed reading of the 1993 essay, pp. 3–21, not a full primary reading.
proposed_edges.map_label: Challenges the exclusion of U.S. empire

proposed_edges.relationship: In Commentary: Domesticating Foreign Policy (1994), Kaplan used cultural studies’ examination of disciplinary boundaries to question the separation of domestic and foreign relations in historical analysis.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Publisher-displayed extract, opening two paragraphs of p. 97, read: disciplines are ‘social constructions or representations’, and the symposium questions domestic/foreign separation. This is a methodological contribution mapped to New cultural history, not membership in a single school. Remaining pp. 98–105 unread; no position assigned to an unnamed symposium participant.
proposed_edges.map_label: Cultural analysis across domestic and foreign

proposed_edges.relationship: Stoler’s acknowledgments to Haunted by Empire (2006) credit Kaplan with helping plan the collection in spring 2002, while recording that Kaplan withdrew before publication.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Authorized publisher preview, acknowledgments pp. xv–xvi (PDF pages 16–17): Stoler names Kaplan among those meeting at NYU to plan contributors and an organic exchange; p. xvi lists ‘some departed (Amy Kaplan)’. Intellectual planning collaboration explicitly documented. No coeditorship, coauthorship or chapter in the published volume claimed. Undirected collaborative connection; later published chapters unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Tense and Tender Ties (2001; read in its 2006 reprint), Stoler treats Kaplan’s three absences in Left Alone with America (1993) as illuminating an earlier historiography but qualifies their continuing scope in light of newer research.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Authorized 2006 preview, pp. 26–27 (PDF pages 47–48), crosscurrents section: the earlier diagnosis was ‘instructive and productively disquieting’, but its ‘timely assessment was of another moment’. The following paragraph identifies subsequent research bridging those divisions. Qualified historiographical criticism, not denial of Kaplan’s earlier importance. Copyright leaf confirms original Journal of American History publication in December 2001; that original version not independently read.
proposed_edges.map_label: Qualifies the reach of the three absences

proposed_edges.relationship: In Revisiting Dollar Diplomacy: Narratives of Money and Manliness (1998), Emily S. Rosenberg drew on Kaplan and Donald E. Pease's Cultures of United States Imperialism (1993) as the cultural-history strand of her effort to bring economic history and cultural analysis together in studying U.S. foreign relations.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the publisher's indexed article text, including the methodological paragraph and note 6. The direct page open failed. This is a stated methodological resource, not a claim that Kaplan originated Rosenberg's research or supplied its empirical findings.
proposed_edges.map_label: Cultural analysis in the study of dollar diplomacy

proposed_edges.relationship: According to Alex Lubin’s welcome to the 2025 ASA meeting, Matthew Frye Jacobson’s 2012 ASA presidential address re-articulated the case Amy Kaplan made in her own presidential address, “Violent Belongings and the Question of Empire Today” (2003; published 2004), for thinking of the United States as an empire, while recognizing that empire had entered a different, neoliberal phase.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Lubin explicitly describes Jacobson's continuation and revision of Kaplan's argument. Evidence is the association's retrospective account; Jacobson's complete address remains unread. The publisher excerpt of Brickhouse and Gillman's introduction, pp. 7–8, corroborates his turn to neoliberal empire but labels the conference year 2013; use the ASA's 2012 delivery date.

proposed_edges.relationship: Michael J. Hogan's The Next Big Thing: The Future of Diplomatic History in a Global Age (2004) identifies Kaplan and Donald E. Pease's Cultures of United States Imperialism (1993) as an early landmark in American studies' turn toward transnational and international inquiry.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the publisher's indexed article text and note 19; the direct page open failed. The field mapping records a named contribution to transnational inquiry, not the founding of global history or influence on every participant in that field.
proposed_edges.map_label: Imperial culture in the transnational turn
